reading.rtitle: How We Run the People Call
paras: This note goes to everybody who joins the monthly people call for the first time. The call is twenty minutes long and it has never once run over. That is not discipline, it is design, and the design is written down here so that nobody has to guess.

The agenda is sent the night before with a time next to each item, and the person who owns the item is named on the agenda, not chosen in the meeting. If your name is on an item, you open it. You are expected to lead with the number and not with the adjective: attrition is fourteen per cent and rising, not attrition is a concern. If something needs a decision on the call, say so in your first sentence, because a decision requested at minute nineteen is a decision postponed.

Anything that cannot be answered in the room is parked. Parking is not refusing. The chair writes the parked question into the follow-up with an owner and a date, and the follow-up goes out the same afternoon. Two rules protect this: nobody may park their own question, and no question may be parked twice.

On interruption, the guidance is the opposite of what most new participants expect. Waiting for a gap does not read as courtesy here; it reads as absence. Say the name of the person you are cutting into, say how long you need, and then take exactly that long. The chair will bring in anybody who has not spoken by minute fifteen, but nobody should have to be brought in.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- internal guidance written for this lesson

choices: To explain to new participants how one recurring meeting is run, and why.
To announce that the monthly people call is being replaced by a written report.
To report the retention numbers discussed on the last people call.

items: The owner of each agenda item is decided during the call.
The note says the owner is named on the agenda, not chosen in the meeting.
A question that cannot be answered in the room is written into the follow-up with an owner and a date.
The note says parking is not refusing, and that the chair writes the parked question into the follow-up with an owner and a date.
Participants are told to bring the adjective before the number.
The note says the opposite: lead with the number and not with the adjective.
Waiting for a gap before speaking is treated as good manners on this call.
The note says waiting for a gap does not read as courtesy here, it reads as absence.
The same question cannot be parked on two separate calls.
The note says no question may be parked twice.

items.situation: Open the call. First sentence, in one breath.
tips: Let us get started -- three things on the agenda and twenty minutes.
Time first. It is what buys you the right to cut people off later.

items.situation: Somebody asks a legal question nobody can answer. Say your move.
tips: I would rather park that until we have the legal answer.
Park it, name an owner, and put it in the follow-up.

items.situation: Greg is mid-sentence and you have a fact he needs. Cut in.
tips: Greg, can I add one thing there? Two minutes and I will stop.
Name first, then the length. Never apologise.

items.situation: You want finance in the room on this question. Say it.
tips: Let me loop in Marcus before we answer that one.
Loop in, not call or invite.

items.situation: Your team cannot take a second project this quarter. Say it without saying no.
tips: My team does not have the bandwidth for a second rollout this quarter.
Bandwidth is the word that makes it a fact instead of a refusal.

items.situation: Close the call in one sentence.
tips: Two action items, both mine, and the follow-up goes out this afternoon.
Owners and a time. Nothing else.

listenings.text: Good morning everyone, let us get started, we have twenty minutes and I want to protect them. Three things on the agenda today. Retention for the quarter, the onboarding redesign, and the hiring plan for the two new sites. I am going to ask Patricia to take the first two, and I will take the third. Two ground rules, because we have new people on this call. If you have a number, say the number, not the adjective. And if something needs a decision today, say so when you start, not when you finish. Anything that does not need a decision today, we park and I put it in the follow-up. Patricia, over to you, retention first.

The thing nobody tells you about American meetings is that waiting for a gap is not polite, it is invisible. There is no gap. People come in over the top of each other and nobody takes offence. What I did for the first year was wait, and at the end of the call somebody would say, we did not hear from you. So here is what I do now. I say the person name first. Greg, can I add one thing there. That is it. The name buys you half a second and half a second is all you need. The second trick is to say how long you will take. Two minutes on this and then I will stop. People let you in when they know when you will get out. And if you are cut off yourself, do not apologise. Just say, let me finish this point, and finish it.
